source_text: De genu quoque ponendo uarietatem obseruationis patitur oratio per pauculos quosdam qui sabbato abstinent genibus. quae dissensio cum maxime apud ecclesias causam dicit, dominus dabit gratiam suam, ut aut cedant aut sine aliorum scandalo sententia sua utantur. nos uero, sicut accepimus, solo die dominicae resurrectionis non ab isto tantum, sed omni anxietatis habitu et officio cauere debemus differentes etiam negotia, ne quem diabolo locum demus. tantundem et spatio Pentecostes, quae eadem exultationis sollemnitate dispungitur. ceterum omni die quis dubitet prosternere se deo uel prima saltem oratione qua lucem ingredimur? ieiuniis autem et stationibus nulla oratio sine genu et reliquo humilitatis more celebranda est. non enim oramus tantum, sed et deprecamur et satisfacimus deo domino nostro. de temporibus orationis nihil omnino praescriptum est, nisi plane omni in tempore et loco orare.
thought_title: When and how to kneel in prayer
orientation: Tertullian is giving practical rules for the bodily posture and times of Christian prayer, after discussing the veiling of virgins.
pass_a_gloss: About the knee also being placed, prayer suffers a variety of observance through a very few certain people who on the Sabbath abstain from the knees. Since this disagreement especially among the churches pleads its cause, the Lord will give his grace, so that they either yield or use their own opinion without scandal to others. But we, just as we have received, on the day alone of the Lord's resurrection ought to refrain not only from this, but from every habit and duty of anxiety, deferring also business affairs, lest we give any place to the devil. The same also for the space of Pentecost, which is discharged with the same solemnity of exultation. But on every other day who would hesitate to prostrate himself to God, at least with the first prayer by which we enter the light? But on fasts and fast days no prayer is to be celebrated without the knee and the rest of the manner of humility. For we do not only pray, but we also entreat and make satisfaction to God our Lord. About the times of prayer nothing at all has been prescribed, except plainly to pray at every time and place.

choices.english: prayer suffers a variety of observance
choices.why: Keeps the literal force of patitur (suffers/undergoes) and the abstract noun phrase, preserving Tertullian's slightly awkward Latin idiom.
rejected: there is variation in the practice of prayer

choices.why: Literal legal idiom; Tertullian frames the disagreement as a case being argued.

choices.english: on the day alone of the Lord's resurrection
choices.why: Preserves the emphatic position of solo (alone) and the literal genitive construction.

choices.english: from every habit and duty of anxiety
choices.why: Literal rendering of habitu and officio as habit and duty, keeping the paired nouns.
rejected: from every anxious posture and activity
from all anxious demeanor and business

choices.why: Literal sense of dispungitur as settled/completed, preserving the unusual verb.

choices.english: by which we enter the light
choices.why: Literal rendering of the relative clause; lucem means daylight, the start of the day.
rejected: with which we begin the day

pass_b_english: As for kneeling, prayer also allows some variety in practice because of a few people who refrain from kneeling on the Sabbath. Since this disagreement is currently being argued especially in the churches, the Lord will grant his grace so that they either yield or hold their opinion without causing others to stumble.

But we ourselves, as we have received the tradition, should refrain from kneeling on the day of the Lord's resurrection alone. And not only from kneeling, but from every posture and activity of anxiety. We should also postpone our business affairs, so that we give no place to the devil. The same applies to the whole period of Pentecost, which is marked by the same joyful celebration.

On every other day, who would hesitate to prostrate himself before God, at least in the first prayer with which we enter the daylight? On days of fasting and on fast days, no prayer should be offered without kneeling and the rest of the humble manner. For we do not merely pray, but we entreat and make satisfaction to God our Lord.
About the times of prayer, nothing at all has been prescribed, except plainly to pray at every time and in every place.

problems.quote: On every other day, who would hesitate to prostrate himself before God
problems.source_quote: ceterum omni die quis dubitet prosternere se deo
problems.why: English adds "other", restricting "omni die" (every day) to only some days.
problems.fix: On every day, who would hesitate to prostrate himself before God
problems.ruling: 'ceterum omni die' means 'but on every day'; adding 'other' after excluding Sunday/Pentecost changes the universal scope.

fixed: Changed 'On every other day' to 'On every day' because the source 'ceterum omni die' means 'but on every day', not 'every other day'.

polish.changed: Clarified the contrast between the Lord's day and every other day, distinguished the two fasting observances, and broke the long passage into shorter paragraphs that follow the turns of thought.

notes.quote: the day of the Lord's resurrection

variants.text: the day of the Lord's resurrection

notes.why: 'Easter' and 'the day of the Lord's resurrection' are the same day; 'Pentecost' here is the season, not the feast.
notes.fix: Note that Easter = the Lord's resurrection day and Pentecost = the fifty-day season.

notes.why: Reader cannot tell whether 'fast day,' 'days of fasting,' and 'the fast' are the same or different observances.
notes.fix: Distinguish 'station/fast day' (appointed congregational fast) from personal fasting.
